title: Order & Ranking
summary: Rank-conversion and ordering puzzles: ranks from either end, totals from two ranks, people between two positions, queue shifts, and taller/heavier comparison chains. Two formulas (n + 1 − p and a + b − 1) plus the between-count run the entire numeric half; the comparison half is inequality chaining into one unique order. Speed comes from drawing a mini-row and from the built-in check a + b = n + 1.

subtopics.title: How ranking questions work
subtopics.concept:
People (or objects) stand in a line or carry ranks, and you must convert between viewpoints: top↔bottom, left↔right, front↔back. The entire topic runs on two ideas:

1. **Mirror conversion**: if there are $n$ positions, the person at position $p$ from one end sits at position $n + 1 - p$ from the other. The '+1' exists because the person's own seat is counted on both sides.
2. **Two-viewpoint total**: if the same person is $a$-th from one end and $b$-th from the other, then $n = a + b - 1$.

Everything else — 'how many between', overlaps, joined queues — is these two formulas plus careful reading. Draw a tiny line of boxes for any question that involves three or more people; the 5 seconds of drawing prevents every 'off by one' answer.

formulas.name: Total from two ranks
formulas.note: Same person, ranked from both ends.

formulas.name: Between count
formulas.note: Two positions measured from the SAME end.

tricks.title: Draw the end-zones
tricks.body: Sketch a short row of boxes. Fill in what you know at the ends: 'a-th from left' means a−1 people before her. Counting the unknowns at each end replaces every formula with a picture.

example.q:
**Q.** In a row of 40, A is 11th from the left. How many are to her right?

**Sol.** 11th from left → 10 before her; 40 − 11 = **29 to her right** (she is 30th from the right).
example.solution: a-th from an end = (a−1) people beyond that end. The rest is subtraction.

mistakes: Forgetting the +1/−1 corrections — the examiner sets traps exactly one away from the answer.
Mixing viewpoints: subtracting a 'from the right' rank from a 'from the left' rank directly.
Assuming the answer must be one less or one more than a listed option — compute first.
subtopics.notes:
### Rank, position and order: the three conversions

Every question here involves a line of people (or a stack of objects) and a rank measured from one end. Three facts convert anything into anything.

**Fact 1 — the two ends are mirrors.** In a row of T people, the person r-th from the left is $(T - r + 1)$-th from the right. Example: 10th from the left in a row of 40 → $40 - 10 + 1$ = 31st from the right. The +1 exists because the person is counted once at each end.

**Fact 2 — two ranks make the total.** If one person is a-th from one end and b-th from the other end, the row holds

$$T = a + b - 1$$

Again the −1: the person was counted in both numbers. Example: 9th from the left and 11th from the right → $9 + 11 - 1$ = 19 people.

**Fact 3 — a swap copies positions.** When two people interchange places, each simply takes over the other's seat. To find a new rank, convert the other person's rank into the same end first: Shyam 9th from the right in a row of 25 → $25 - 9 + 1$ = 17th from the left; after a swap, Ram sits 17th from the left.

**Stacks and rows of objects.** Books, boxes and shelves follow the same logic vertically: 'above' is like 'to the left'. The only new skill is assembling a scattered description into one ordered list — draw the order top to bottom as each sentence arrives, then read the asked slot.

**Facing direction changes everything.** A row facing north has its left and right in the usual sense; a row facing **south** has them swapped (their left is your right). Questions flag this deliberately — underline the facing word before using any left/right clue.

**People ahead vs behind.** In a queue of T, a person r-th from the front has $r - 1$ people ahead and $T - r$ behind. The −1 on 'ahead' (the person is not ahead of themselves) is the most common slip in the whole topic.

### Quick revision
- Mirror: r-th from one end = $(T - r + 1)$ from the other.
- Total: $T = a + b - 1$ for ranks a and b from opposite ends of the same person.
- Swap: convert both people to the same end; each takes the other's number.
- Ahead = r − 1; behind = T − r.
- Facing south flips left/right — read the facing word first.

**Why the formulas work (and why that matters).** Every shortcut in this topic is bookkeeping on one sentence: *a rank is one more than the number of people before you.* The mirror formula is that sentence counted from the other side (the people before you become the people after you, plus you); the total formula is the two before-counts overlapping on you, hence −1. When an exam twists the wording ('four people between them', 'equal number ahead and behind'), derive the equation from this sentence instead of memorising a new formula — it takes ten seconds and never breaks.

**The twisted variants worth pre-solving.** 'Equal ahead and behind' → $r - 1 = T - r$ → $T = 2r - 1$. 'k people between A and B, same end' → $b = a + k + 1$. 'A is exactly in the middle of an odd row' → $r = (T+1)/2$. Practise these three derivations once and the variants stop costing time.

patterns.name: Rank flips between the two ends
patterns.howToSpot: One rank and the total are given; the same person's rank from the other end is asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Other end = total − rank + 1.
2. Keep the +1: the person sits at both counts.
3. For queues: ahead = rank − 1, behind = total − rank.

*Why it works:* the two counts meet at the same person.

example.q: **In a row of 40 students, Ravi is 10th from the left. What is his position from the right?**
example.solution: $40 - 10 + 1$ = **31st** from the right.

patterns.name: Total from two opposite ranks
patterns.howToSpot: One person's rank from both ends is given; the size of the row/class is asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Total = a + b − 1.
2. Sanity-check: total ≥ each rank.
3. Works for rows, queues and class ranks alike.

*Why it works:* the person was counted once in each rank; subtract the double count.

example.q: **A student is 23rd from the left and 12th from the right. How many students are in the row?**

patterns.name: Interchange of positions
patterns.howToSpot: Two people swap places; a new rank after the swap is asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Convert the partner's rank to the asked end (mirror if needed).
2. The swapper now holds exactly that converted number.
3. The other person takes the first person's old number.

*Why it works:* a swap is a copy of positions between two people.

example.q: **In a row of 25, Ram is 8th from the left and Shyam is 9th from the right. They swap places. What is Ram's new position from the left?**
example.solution: Shyam's seat: $25 - 9 + 1$ = 17th from the left → Ram now **17th**.

patterns.name: Assembling a scattered stack or row
patterns.howToSpot: Objects/friends described by above-below or left-right clues; a slot or extreme is asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Convert each clue into order arrows (above = >).
2. Merge into one list, drawing as you read.
3. Read the asked slot off the finished list.

*Why it works:* scattered clues describe one total order; drawing recovers it.

example.q: **Red is above Blue; Green is below Blue but above White; Yellow is at the bottom. Which box is at the top?**
example.solution: Red > Blue > Green > White > Yellow → top = **Red**.

subtopics.title: Ranks and positions
subtopics.concept:
Single-person rank conversions and totals:

- **Convert an end**: 12th from top in a class of 45 → 45 + 1 − 12 = 34th from bottom.
- **Find the total**: 8th from the left and 21st from the right → n = 8 + 21 − 1 = 28.
- **'Same from both ends'**: 11th from either end → n = 11 + 11 − 1 = 21.

Watch the exam's phrasing variants: 'how many students scored less than him' = his rank **from the bottom**, 'precedes him' = people before his position, 'queue joined from the front' shifts every old position forward by the number of joiners.

tricks.title: Sanity-span check
tricks.body: The two ranks of one person must satisfy a + b = n + 1. Before marking a total, add the given ranks: if the sum is not total-plus-one, one of the numbers was misread.

example.q:
**Q.** K is 12th from the left and 19th from the right. Total?

**Sol.** 12 + 19 = 31, so n = 31 − 1 = **30**. Check: 12th from left has 11 left of her; 19th from right has 18 right of her; 11 + 1 + 18 = 30 ✓.
example.solution: a + b = n + 1 is a two-second self-check built into every question.

mistakes: Treating '11th from either end' as two different people's ranks.
Missing queue shifts when people join or leave ahead of the person.
subtopics.notes:
### Single-person rank work

This subtopic drills the conversions one person at a time: one end to the other, two ends to the total, and the moving-queue variants where people join or leave.

**The mirror conversion.** From-rank r in a row of T: other end = $T - r + 1$. Practical route: rank from bottom = class size − rank from top + 1. A 23rd-from-the-top rank in a class of 60 is 38th from the bottom: $60 - 23 + 1 = 38$.

**The total from two ends.** When the question gives one person's rank from both ends, the class size pops out: $T = a + b - 1$. Sonu 14th from the left and 20th from the right → $14 + 20 - 1 = 33$ people. Sanity-check the answer: it must be at least as big as each rank.

**Queues that change size.** People joining the front shift everyone back; people leaving the front pull everyone forward. Rule: adjust the *number of people before the person* first, then add one.
- k people join **ahead** of you → new rank = old + k.
- k people **leave from ahead** of you → new rank = old − k.
- If the joiners/leavers are behind you, your rank does not change.

**People leaving mid-queue.** '5 people left the row from the left side': anyone to the right of them slides left by 5. A person 16th from the left becomes 11th. Anyone to the **left** of the departed block keeps their rank but the total shrinks.

**Ranks from both ends together.** Some questions hand you rank from the top *and* from the bottom of a class with a twist ('A is 12th from the top and 41st from the bottom; how many students are there?'). Same formula: $12 + 41 - 1 = 52$.

**Watch the units.** 'Rank' counts the person; 'people ahead/behind' does not. Convert explicitly: ahead = rank − 1; rank = ahead + 1. Questions swap these words between the question and the options on purpose.

### Quick revision
- Other end: $T - r + 1$. Two ends: $T = a + b - 1$.
- Joiners ahead: rank + k. Leavers ahead: rank − k. Changes behind you: no change.
- Mid-row exits: slide only people to the right of the exit block.
- ahead = rank − 1, behind = T − rank; convert words to numbers before computing.

**Two-sided puzzles.** Harder variants give a rank from one end plus a second fact ('he is exactly midway', 'there are 3 people between him and the front'). Convert the fact into a before-count first: 'midway' means ahead = behind; '3 between him and the front' means ahead = 4. Once the before-count is known, rank = before + 1 and the total follows if the other side is described.

**Class ranks vs rows.** The formulas are identical; only the words move (top/bottom instead of left/right, pass/fail groups at the ends). One warning: 'X failed' questions where 'rank from the bottom among failures' is asked — strip the failed students out of the total before mirroring. The formula never changes, but the total does.

patterns.name: Rank from the other end
patterns.howToSpot: Class/queue size known; rank from top/left/front given; the mirror rank is asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Apply total − rank + 1.
2. Read the end words carefully (top↔bottom, left↔right, front↔back).

*Why it works:* the two counts meet at the same person.

example.q: **In a class of 60, Neha ranks 23rd from the top. What is her rank from the bottom?**

patterns.name: Total from two ranks
patterns.howToSpot: One person's rank from both ends is given; the total is asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Add the ranks, subtract 1.
2. Check the total is not smaller than either rank.

*Why it works:* the shared person is counted twice.

example.q: **Sonu is 14th from the left and 20th from the right in a row. How many people are in the row?**

patterns.name: Queue joining and leaving
patterns.howToSpot: People join or leave a queue; the person's new position is asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Count only people **ahead**: rank = (people ahead) + 1.
2. k join ahead → +k; k leave from ahead → −k.
3. Changes behind the person never move their rank.

*Why it works:* a rank is one more than the number of people ahead.

example.q: **In a queue of 35, Moni is 12th. If 8 people ahead of her leave, what is her new position?**

patterns.name: Rank after people leave mid-row
patterns.howToSpot: Some people exit from one side of a standing row; a survivor's new rank is asked.
patterns.logic:
1. If the exits are to the person's left, subtract the count.
2. If they are to the right, the rank from the left is unchanged.
3. Recompute the total if it is asked.

*Why it works:* survivors slide toward the emptied side.

example.q: **A is 16th from the left in a row of 40. If 5 people leave from the left end, what is A's new rank from the left?**
example.solution: The 5 departed were all ahead of A → $16 - 5$ = **11th**.

subtopics.title: People between two positions
subtopics.concept:
Three standard shapes:

1. **Both from the same end**: between = |a − b| − 1.
2. **From opposite ends**: convert one rank first (position from the other end = n + 1 − p), then subtract.
3. **Overlapping ranks**: A is 10th from the left, B is 25th from the left, in a row of 20 — impossible unless ranks overlap; the between-count formula still works after conversion, but the exam usually avoids true contradictions.

For the **'middle person'** variant (odd gap), the middle position between ranks a and b (same end) is (a + b) ÷ 2 — it must come out as a whole number; if it does not, the question intends 'two middle people' and asks something else.

tricks.title: Convert, then count
tricks.body: Never subtract ranks from different ends. Convert one with n + 1 − p, then |a − b| − 1.

example.q:
**Q.** Row of 30: A is 10th from the left, B is 12th from the right. How many sit between?

**Sol.** B from the left = 30 + 1 − 12 = 19th. Between = 19 − 10 − 1 = **8**.
example.solution: One conversion, one subtraction, one final −1.

mistakes: Subtracting a left-rank from a right-rank directly.
Dropping the final −1 (counting the endpoints themselves).
Using n + 1 − p twice, converting both ranks.
subtopics.notes:
### Counting between two people

Four shapes cover every 'how many between' question. Know which end each rank comes from — that decides the formula.

**Shape 1 — both ranks from the same end.** A is a-th and B is b-th from the left:

$$\text{between} = |a - b| - 1$$

The gap shrinks by one because 'between' excludes both people. Example: 9th and 26th from the top → 16 between.

**Shape 2 — ranks from opposite ends.** Convert one rank to the shared end first, or use the total. In a row of T with P a-th from the left and Q b-th from the right:

$$\text{between} = T - a - b$$

Example: row of 45, X 14th from the left, Y 18th from the right → $45 - 14 - 18 = 13$. If the total is not given, build it with $a + b - 1$ from any person who has both ranks.

**Shape 3 — the middle person.** Both from the same end a and b: the midpoint rank is $(a + b) / 2$ from that end. 9th and 21st from the left → the middle person is 15th from the left. If a + b is odd, the exact middle is a half-position — exams phrase those as 'immediately between', and the two neighbours are $(a+b-1)/2$ and $(a+b+1)/2$.

**Shape 4 — the overlap deduction.** The classic: 'Ram is 17th from the left, Shyam 9th from the right; after interchanging, Ram is 22nd from the left.' Ram takes Shyam's seat, keeping Shyam's from-right rank (9): total $= 22 + 9 - 1 = 30$. Then Shyam's old seat was $30 - 9 + 1 = 22$nd from the left, and the original gap is $22 - 17 - 1 = 4$. Overlap questions always split into: build the total first, then run a plain Shape 1 or 2 count.

**Sanity checks.** Between-counts can never be negative — a negative answer means the two ranks described the same person or the ranks were from ends you did not account for. And between + 2 ≤ total: the two people themselves exist too.

### Quick revision
- Same end: $|a-b| - 1$. Opposite ends (total T): $T - a - b$.
- Middle person (same end): $(a+b)/2$ from that end.
- Overlap puzzles: recover T first ($a' + b' - 1$), then count between.
- Convert every rank to the same end before subtracting; 'between' excludes both people.
- Negative gap = misread ends; stop and re-convert.

**A worked flow for exam speed.** Read the question once, labelling each rank with its end (L/R or T/B) and circling the total if present. Then one line of arithmetic:
- same end → subtract, drop 2 (|a−b| − 1);
- opposite ends → subtract from the total;
- no total → build it from any both-ends person (a + b − 1).
Under exam pressure the labelling step is what prevents the classic error of subtracting ranks that came from different ends.

**Between-counts with a twist.** Questions sometimes ask 'how many people do NOT lie between them' (= total − between − 2) or 'what fraction of the row lies between'. Both are one extra subtraction on the between-count — compute between first, always, then answer the actual question.

patterns.name: Between, same end
patterns.howToSpot: Both ranks measured from the same end (top, left, front).
patterns.logic:
1. Between = |a − b| − 1.
2. 'Between' excludes both named people.
3. Absolute value: either rank may be bigger.

*Why it works:* the gap between two positions minus the two endpoints.

example.q: **R ranks 9th from the top and S ranks 26th from the top. How many students are between them?**

patterns.name: Between, opposite ends
patterns.howToSpot: One rank from the left/top, the other from the right/bottom, total known.
patterns.logic:
1. Between = total − rank1 − rank2.
2. If no total is given, build one from a both-ends person first.
3. Negative result = you misread the ends.

*Why it works:* subtract both people and the ends from the row.

example.q: **In a row of 45, X is 14th from the left and Y is 18th from the right. How many people are between them?**

patterns.name: Middle person between two ranks
patterns.howToSpot: 'Who/which position is exactly in the middle of A and B?'
patterns.logic:
1. Convert both ranks to the same end.
2. Middle position = (a + b) / 2 from that end.
3. Odd sum → the two immediate neighbours share the middle; read the options.

*Why it works:* the midpoint of two positions is their average.

example.q: **A is 9th from the left and B is 21st from the left. Which position is exactly in the middle?**
example.solution: $(9 + 21)/2$ = **15th from the left**.

patterns.name: Overlap: swap reveals the total
patterns.howToSpot: A swap or second measurement exposes a rank the row never stated; count between in the original line.
patterns.logic:
1. The swapped person keeps the partner's from-end rank: total = new rank + partner's rank − 1.
2. Convert everyone to one end.
3. Between = |a − b| − 1 as usual.

*Why it works:* the swap pins a second measurement to the same seat, fixing the row size.

example.q: **Ram is 17th from the left, Shyam 9th from the right. After interchanging, Ram is 22nd from the left. How many students sat between them originally?**
example.solution: Total $= 22 + 9 - 1 = 30$. Shyam's old seat = $30 - 9 + 1 = 22$nd from the left. Between = $22 - 17 - 1$ = **4**.

subtopics.title: Ordering and comparison chains
subtopics.concept:
'P is taller than Q but shorter than R… who is second tallest?' The constraints sort a small set — five people, five or six statements. The reliable method:

1. Write each statement as an inequality fragment: 'P taller than Q' → P > Q.
2. Chain all fragments into one ordering, or brute-force by hand when fragments branch.
3. Read the answer from the final chain.

A complete CGL puzzle always has a **unique** chain. If two orderings satisfy your reading of the statements, you misread one — usually 'X is taller than Y' vs 'Y is taller than X', or a hidden 'immediately taller'. Note the special comparatives: 'immediately above' fixes adjacency; 'between A and B' fixes position, not just inequality.

tricks.title: Longest-chain first
tricks.body: Find the person who appears in the most statements and build outwards from them. The chain assembles in one pass instead of three.

example.q:
**Q.** A > B; C > A; D > C but D < E. Order?

**Sol.** Chain the A–C–D–E spine: E > D > C > A > B — unique. Middle (third tallest) = **C**.
example.solution: Start from the most-mentioned name; attach the rest one fragment at a time.

mistakes: Answering from a partial chain before all statements are used.
Accepting two possible orders without re-reading the statements.
subtopics.notes:
### 'Taller than, older than, scored more than': ranking from clues

These puzzles give scattered comparisons and ask for a slot: tallest, second oldest, least scorer. The method is always the same — merge the clues into one ordered line, then read it.

**The chain-building routine.**
1. Write each clue as an arrow: 'A is taller than B' → A > B.
2. Join arrows that share a head or tail into one long chain. A > B and B > D merges to A > B > D.
3. Where the chain is under-determined (two people never compared), the answer is 'cannot be determined' — but check the question first: many slots are fixed even when the full order is not.
4. Read the asked slot from the finished chain: tallest = left end, shortest = right end, second tallest = second from the left.

**Marks and scores.** 'Scored more' behaves exactly like 'taller'. Beware the reversed words: 'fewer than', 'younger than', 'less than' point the arrow the other way. Convert every clue into > arrows pointing at the *better/bigger/older* person before merging.

**Under-determined traps.** Five clues about four people can still leave a free pair: 'A > B, C > D' says nothing about A vs C. If the question asks for the tallest and only one candidate can possibly top the chain (everyone else has someone above them), the answer stands even without a total order. Rule: fix the slot, not necessarily the list.

**Objects in columns and shelves.** 'The red box is above the blue box' is a comparison with the arrow pointing up. Stack the chain top to bottom and read positions ('third from the top') exactly as you read 'second tallest'.

**Facing pairs.** Two people facing **each other** (like a north-facing and a south-facing person) have opposite left/right directions: the north-facing person's left is the south-facing person's right. Draw the two arrows before using any such clue.

### Quick revision
- Every clue → an arrow toward the bigger/older/better; join arrows into one chain.
- Read the slot: tallest = chain head, Nth = Nth from the head.
- Reversed words (less, younger, fewer, shorter) flip the arrow — convert first.
- A slot is answerable when only one person can fill it, even if the whole order is open.
- Stacks: 'above' is the arrow; facing pairs have mirrored left/right.

**Extraction habits that prevent wrong chains.** Rewrite every clue as a two-symbol line before thinking: 'Sunil is younger than Vijay' → S < V. Keep the inequality signs pointing the same way throughout (bigger/older/higher on the left). Most wrong answers here come from reading a reversed sentence ('younger than', 'fewer than', 'below') in its surface direction — the rewrite step makes the reversal visible.

**When options expose the shortcut.** If two options share a person ('C' and 'C is second oldest'), the chain probably pins that person; test the slot directly: can anyone else occupy slot 2? If nobody can, stop building the chain and mark the answer — total order is a luxury, the slot is the requirement.

patterns.name: Height/size chain to a slot
patterns.howToSpot: 'A is taller than B...' — find the tallest, shortest or an exact slot.
patterns.logic:
1. Write each clue as an arrow toward the taller.
2. Merge into one chain; read slot from the end.
3. If a pair is never compared but only one person can top the chain, that person is the answer.

*Why it works:* 'taller than' is a total-order arrow; chains merge head to tail.

example.q: **A is taller than B; C is taller than A; D is shorter than B. Who is the shortest?**
example.solution: C > A > B > D → shortest = **D**.

patterns.name: Marks ranking
patterns.howToSpot: 'Scored more/less than' clues; highest, lowest or Nth scorer is asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Convert 'scored less' clues so all arrows point toward more marks.
2. Merge; read the slot from the top end.
3. Double-check nobody outside the chain could beat the head.

*Why it works:* scores order exactly like heights.

example.q: **A scored more than B; C scored less than D; B scored more than D. Who scored the least?**
example.solution: A > B > D > C → least = **C**.

patterns.name: Age ranking
patterns.howToSpot: 'Older/younger than' clues about three to six people.
patterns.logic:
1. Point every arrow at the older person.
2. Merge and read: oldest at the head, youngest at the tail.
3. Watch 'younger' — it reverses the sentence's surface order.

*Why it works:* ages are another total order.

example.q: **Rahul is older than Vijay; Sunil is younger than Vijay; Anil is older than Rahul. Who is the youngest?**
example.solution: Anil > Rahul > Vijay > Sunil → youngest = **Sunil**.

patterns.name: Stacked objects and shelves
patterns.howToSpot: Boxes/books/subjects with above-below clues; a slot from the top or bottom is asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Treat 'above' as > pointing upward.
2. Build the stack top to bottom on paper.
3. Slots: Nth from the top = Nth of the list; from the bottom = mirror.

*Why it works:* vertical stacks obey the same order logic as lines.

example.q: **Civics is below Geography; History is below Economics but above Geography; Political Science is at the bottom. Which subject is third from the top?**
example.solution: Economics > History > Geography > Civics > Political Science → third = **Geography**.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Rank conversion at the two ends
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A rank from one end plus a total; the other end is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: Mirror: total − rank + 1; queues: ahead = rank − 1, behind = total − rank.

example.q: **In a queue of 60, S is 21st from the front. How many people are behind her?**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: One person's rank from both ends; class size asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: Add the ranks and subtract 1; the shared person was counted twice.

example.q: **A is 9th from the left and 11th from the right. How many people are in the row?**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'How many between A and B' with ranks from the same or opposite ends.
pyqPatterns.approach: Same end: |a − b| − 1. Opposite ends with total T: T − a − b. Convert ends before subtracting.

example.q: **P is 11th from the left and Q is 9th from the right in a row of 30. How many sit between?**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Who is exactly in the middle of A and B?'
pyqPatterns.approach: Convert to the same end; the midpoint is (a + b) / 2 from that end.

example.q: **Manish is 14th from the left; Rakesh is 8th from the right in a row of 35. Who is midway between them?**
example.solution: Rakesh = $35 - 8 + 1 = 28$th from the left; midway = $(14 + 28)/2$ = **21st from the left**.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Comparison chain to a named slot
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Taller/older/more-marks clues; tallest, youngest or Nth is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: Arrows toward the bigger/older/better; merge into a chain; read the slot; reversed words flip the arrow.

example.q: **M > N; O < N; P > M; Q < O. Who is second highest?**
example.solution: P > M > N > O > Q → second highest = **M**.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Above/below clues for boxes, books or shelves; a slot is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: Above = arrow up; stack the chain on paper; read 'Nth from top' directly off the list.

example.q: **Red above Blue; Green below Blue but above White; Yellow at the bottom. Which is second from the top?**
example.solution: Red, Blue, Green, White, Yellow → second = **Blue**.

solvedExamples.q: In a class of **40 students**, Meena ranks **15th from the top**. What is her rank from the bottom?
solvedExamples.solution: Rank from the other end = 40 + 1 − 15 = **26th**. (25th forgets the +1.)

solvedExamples.q: In a row of students, **Karan is 12th from the left and 19th from the right.** How many students are in the row?
solvedExamples.solution: n = 12 + 19 − 1 = **30**. Check: 11 students left of him + Karan + 18 to his right = 30 ✓.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Add the two ranks, subtract one.

solvedExamples.q: **A is taller than B. C is taller than A. D is taller than C but shorter than E.** Who is the **third tallest**?
solvedExamples.solution: Chain the statements: E > D > C > A > B. Third tallest = **C**. (The chain is forced — each statement slots exactly one person.)
solvedExamples.shortcut: Build one chain E > D > C > A > B and read the slot; no trial and error needed.

solvedExamples.q: In a row of **36 students, A is 15th from the left and B is 9th from the right.** How many students sit **between** A and B?
solvedExamples.shortcut: Convert the right-rank to a left-rank first; then difference minus one.

practice.q: In a class of **45 students, Ravi ranks 12th from the top**. What is his rank from the bottom?
In a row of students, **Sita is 8th from the left and 21st from the right.** How many students are in the row?
practice.shortcut: Sum of the two ranks minus 1.

practice.q: In a row of **40 students, A is 11th from the left end.** What is A's position from the right end?
practice.shortcut: Mirror formula n + 1 − p.

practice.q: In a row of **30 students, A is 10th from the left and B is 12th from the right.** How many students are **between** A and B?
practice.solution: B from the left = 30 + 1 − 12 = 19th. Between = 19 − 10 − 1 = **8**.
practice.shortcut: Convert B to a left-rank, subtract, drop the endpoints.

practice.q: In a queue of **50 people, X is 16th from the front and Y is 20th from the back.** How many people are **between** X and Y?
practice.solution: Y from the front = 50 + 1 − 20 = 31st. Between = 31 − 16 − 1 = **14**.
practice.shortcut: Same-end conversion first; then difference − 1.

practice.q: In a queue, **A is 9th from the front and B is 21st from the front.** Who stands **exactly in the middle** of A and B (in position, not count)?
practice.solution: Middle position = (9 + 21) ÷ 2 = **15th from the front**. (The count of people between them is 11 — different question.)
practice.shortcut: Average the two same-end positions.

practice.q: **Bulbul is 11th from either end of a queue.** How many people are in the queue?
practice.solution: n = 11 + 11 − 1 = **21**. (She is the exact middle of an odd-length queue.)
practice.shortcut: 'Either end' means both ranks are the same number.

practice.q: **A is 17th from the left and 18th from the right in a row.** How many people are in the row?
**P is taller than Q but shorter than R. S is the tallest of all. T is shorter than Q.** Who is the **second tallest**?
practice.solution: Chain: S > R > P > Q > T. Second tallest = **R**. (S is fixed at the top by 'tallest of all'; R > P > Q comes from the other statements.)
practice.shortcut: Pin the extreme first ('tallest of all'), then chain the rest.

practice.q: **A is heavier than B. C is lighter than B. D is heavier than A. E is lighter than C.** Who is the **lightest**?
practice.solution: Chain: D > A > B > C > E. Lightest = **E**. (Each 'lighter than' points downward; the chain bottoms out at E.)
practice.shortcut: One chain from the heaviest statement to the lightest; the last name is the answer.

practice.q: In a test, **M scored more than N, O scored less than N, P scored more than M, and Q scored less than M but more than N.** Who scored the **highest**?
practice.solution: Chain: P > M > Q > N > O. Highest = **P**. (Q sits between M and N, exactly as stated.)
practice.shortcut: 'More than' chains head upward; the chain's top is the answer.

practice.q: In a class test, **Mohan ranks 13th from the top and 57th from the bottom.** How many students appeared for the test?
practice.shortcut: a + b − 1, then sanity-check a + b = n + 1.

practice.q: In a queue of 30 people, **A is 9th from the front. If 5 new people join the queue at the front**, what is A's new position from the front?
practice.solution: Every old position shifts back by 5: 9 + 5 = **14th**. (The queue length also grows to 35, but only front-joins affect A's rank.)
practice.shortcut: Front joiners push the tracked person back one-for-one.

practice.q: In a row of **40 students, A is 15th from the left and B is 25th from the left.** If **A and B interchange their positions**, what is **B's new position from the right**?
practice.solution: After the swap B occupies A's old spot: 15th from the left. From the right = 40 + 1 − 15 = **26th**.
practice.shortcut: An interchange just re-labels the two positions — reuse the mirror formula on the new spot.

practice.q: **X is older than Y. Z is younger than W. V is older than X. W is older than V. Y is older than Z.** Who is the **third oldest**?
practice.solution: Chain: W > V > X > Y > Z (W is pinned above V; V above X; X above Y; Y above Z; and Z < W is automatic). Third oldest = **X**.
practice.shortcut: Build the spine W > V > X, then hang Y and Z below X.

practice.q: **In a row of 40 students, Ravi is 10th from the left end. What is his position from the right end?**
practice.solution: Mirror: $40 - 10 + 1$ = **31st** from the right (the +1 counts Ravi himself once).
practice.shortcut: Other end = total − rank + 1.

practice.q: **Meena is 17th from the right end in a queue of 30 people. What is her position from the left end?**
practice.solution: Mirror: $30 - 17 + 1$ = **14th** from the left.
practice.shortcut: The formula works in both directions.

practice.q: **A person is 9th from the left end and 11th from the right end of a row. How many people are in the row?**
practice.solution: Two ranks of the same person: total = $9 + 11 - 1$ = **19** (the −1 removes the double count).

practice.q: **In a row, a student is 23rd from the left and 12th from the right. How many students are in the row?**
practice.solution: Total = $23 + 12 - 1$ = **34** students.
practice.shortcut: Add the ranks, drop one.

practice.q: **In a row of 25 students, Ram is 8th from the left and Shyam is 9th from the right. They interchange places. What is Ram's new position from the left?**
practice.solution: Shyam's seat from the left: $25 - 9 + 1$ = 17th. Ram takes exactly that seat → **17th** from the left.
practice.shortcut: Convert the partner's rank to the asked end; that is the new seat.

practice.q: **In a row of 20 students, Ajay is 7th from the left and Vijay is 12th from the right. If they swap places, what is Vijay's new position from the left?**
practice.solution: Vijay takes Ajay's seat → **7th** from the left. (Ajay moves to Vijay's old seat, 9th from the left.)
practice.shortcut: After a swap each person simply sits where the partner sat.

practice.q: **Five boxes are stacked: Red is above Blue; Green is below Blue but above White; Yellow is at the bottom. Which box is at the top?**
practice.solution: Build top to bottom: Red > Blue > Green > White > Yellow → top = **Red**.
practice.shortcut: 'Above' is an arrow pointing up; stack as you read.

practice.q: **Six books: P is above Q; R is below Q; S is above P; U lies between P and Q; T is at the bottom. Which book is **third from the top**?**
practice.solution: S above P above Q; U between P and Q; R below Q; T last → S, P, U, Q, R, T. Third = **U**.
practice.shortcut: Chain the above/below clues, slot U into the gap, pin T at the bottom.

practice.q: **45 students stand in a row and R is exactly in the middle. What is R's position from the left end?**
practice.solution: Middle of 45: $(45 + 1)/2$ = **23rd**. Check by mirror: $45 - 23 + 1 = 23$ ✓ — the same from both ends.
practice.shortcut: Odd count: middle = (total + 1)/2 from either end.

practice.q: **In a row, A is 7th from the left end and B is 9th from the right end. A and B sit in adjacent positions with nobody between them. How many people are in the row?**
practice.solution: Adjacent → B is immediately after A: B is 8th from the left. Total = B's two ranks: $8 + 9 - 1$ = **16**. Check: A 7th, B 8th, $16 - 9 + 1 = 8$ ✓.
practice.shortcut: Adjacency fixes the second person's other-end rank; then a + b − 1.

practice.q: **Five friends sit in a row: P is to the left of Q; R is to the right of Q; S sits between P and Q; T is at the extreme right. Who sits second from the left?**
practice.solution: P left of Q with S between → P, S, Q; R to the right of Q → P, S, Q, R; T at the extreme right → P, S, Q, R, T. Second = **S**.
practice.shortcut: Chain the left-of clues; the extreme seat pins the last slot.

practice.q: **In a queue of 60 people, S is 21st from the front. How many people are behind her?**
practice.solution: Behind = total − rank = $60 - 21$ = **39** (S herself is not behind).
practice.shortcut: Behind = T − rank; ahead = rank − 1.

practice.q: **In a class of 60 students, Neha ranks 23rd from the top. What is her rank from the bottom?**
practice.solution: $60 - 23 + 1$ = **38th** from the bottom.
practice.shortcut: Bottom rank = size − top rank + 1.

practice.q: **Sonu is 14th from the left end and 20th from the right end of a row. How many people are in the row?**
practice.shortcut: Ranks add to total + 1.

practice.q: **In a queue of 35 people, Moni is 12th from the front. If 8 people ahead of her leave the queue, what is Moni's new position?**
practice.solution: 8 people ahead left → everyone behind them slides forward: $12 - 8$ = **4th** from the front.
practice.shortcut: Leavers ahead of you: rank − k. Leavers behind: no change.

practice.q: **A is 16th from the left in a row of 40 people. If 5 people leave the row from the left end, what is A's new rank from the left?**
practice.solution: The 5 departed were ahead of A (positions 1-5); A slides left by 5 → $16 - 5$ = **11th**.
practice.shortcut: Exits to your left subtract; exits to your right leave your rank alone.

practice.q: **A is 7th from the left end and B is 19th from the left end of a row. How many people are between them?**
practice.solution: Same end: $|19 - 7| - 1$ = **11** people between.
practice.shortcut: Same-end gap minus the two named people.

practice.q: **In a class, R ranks 9th from the top and S ranks 26th from the top. How many students rank between them?**
practice.solution: Same end (top): $|26 - 9| - 1$ = **16** students.
practice.shortcut: Difference of ranks minus one.

practice.q: **P is 11th from the left end and Q is 9th from the right end of a row of 30 people. How many people are between them?**
practice.solution: Opposite ends: $30 - 11 - 9$ = **10** between.
practice.shortcut: Total minus both ranks.

practice.q: **In a row of 45 students, X is 14th from the left and Y is 18th from the right. How many students are between them?**
practice.shortcut: Opposite ends: T − a − b.

practice.q: **A is 9th from the left end and B is 21st from the left end. Which position is exactly in the middle between A and B?**
practice.solution: Midpoint of the same-end ranks: $(9 + 21)/2$ = **15th from the left**.
practice.shortcut: Average of the two positions.

practice.q: **Manish is 14th from the left and Rakesh is 8th from the right in a row of 35. Which position is exactly midway between them?**
practice.solution: Rakesh from the left: $35 - 8 + 1$ = 28th. Midway: $(14 + 28)/2$ = **21st from the left**.
practice.shortcut: Mirror one rank first; then average.

practice.q: **A is 9th from the left end and 16th from the right end of a row. B is 14th from the right end. How many people sit between A and B?**
practice.solution: Row size from A: $9 + 16 - 1$ = 24. B from the left: $24 - 14 + 1$ = 11th. Between A (9th) and B (11th): $|11 - 9| - 1$ = **1** person.
practice.shortcut: Build the total from the both-ends person, convert B, then count.

practice.q: **Ram is 17th from the left and Shyam is 9th from the right in a row. After they interchange places, Ram becomes 22nd from the left. How many students sat between Ram and Shyam originally?**
practice.solution: Ram's new seat is Shyam's old one, still 9th from the right → total = $22 + 9 - 1$ = 30. Shyam's old seat from the left: $30 - 9 + 1$ = 22nd. Between originally: $22 - 17 - 1$ = **4**.
practice.shortcut: The swap pins Ram's seat to both ends → total; then a plain same-end count.

practice.q: **In a class, V ranks 18th from the top and W ranks 31st from the top. How many students lie between them?**
practice.solution: Same end: $|31 - 18| - 1$ = **12** students.
practice.shortcut: Rank difference minus one.

practice.q: **A is taller than B; C is taller than A; D is shorter than B. Who is the shortest?**
practice.solution: Chain: C > A > B > D → shortest = **D**.
practice.shortcut: Arrow toward the taller; the tail of the chain is the shortest.

practice.q: **P is taller than Q; R is shorter than S; Q is taller than S. Who is the tallest?**
practice.solution: Merge: P > Q, Q > S, S > R → P > Q > S > R → tallest = **P**.
practice.shortcut: Chain head = tallest.

practice.q: **In a test, A scored more than B; C scored less than D; B scored more than D. Who scored the least?**
practice.solution: Convert 'less' clues: C < D → D > C. Merge: A > B > D > C → least = **C**.
practice.shortcut: Flip every 'less than' sentence before chaining.

practice.q: **Five students: M scored more than N; O scored fewer than N; P scored more than M; Q scored fewer than O. Who is the second highest scorer?**
practice.solution: Convert: P > M, M > N, N > O, O > Q → P > M > N > O > Q. Second highest = **M**.
practice.shortcut: 'Fewer than' arrows flip; then read slot 2 of the chain.

practice.q: **Rahul is older than Vijay; Sunil is younger than Vijay; Anil is older than Rahul. Who is the youngest?**
practice.solution: Anil > Rahul > Vijay > Sunil → youngest = **Sunil**.
practice.shortcut: 'Younger than' points the arrow the other way; chain and read the tail.

practice.q: **A is older than B but younger than C; D is older than C. Who is the second oldest?**
practice.solution: A > B, C > A, D > C → D > C > A > B → second oldest = **C**.
practice.shortcut: 'Younger than' hides the C > A link — flip it, then merge.

practice.q: **On a shelf: Civics is below Geography; History is below Economics but above Geography; Political Science is at the bottom. Which subject is third from the top?**
practice.solution: Economics > History > Geography > Civics > Political Science → third from the top = **Geography**.
practice.shortcut: 'Below' = lower in the stack; build top-down and read slot 3.

practice.q: **Six poles: A is taller than B; B is taller than C; C is taller than E; E is taller than D; D is taller than F. Which pole is the third tallest?**
practice.solution: A > B > C > E > D > F → third tallest = **C**.
practice.shortcut: One merged chain; third from the head is the answer.

practice.q: **In a queue of 48 people, Mohan is 30th from the front. What is his position from the back?**
practice.solution: $48 - 30 + 1$ = **19th** from the back.
practice.shortcut: Back rank = queue size − front rank + 1.

practice.q: **In a class, Kishan is 18th from the top and 42nd from the bottom. How many students are in the class?**
practice.shortcut: Kishan is counted in both ranks — drop one.

practice.q: **In a queue, Tanvi is 20th from the front. If 12 people join the queue ahead of her, what is her new position from the front?**
practice.solution: 12 people now stand ahead of her who were not there before → $20 + 12$ = **32nd** from the front.
practice.shortcut: Joiners ahead: rank + k. Joiners behind: no change.

practice.q: **In a row of 30 people, B is 12th from the right end. If 4 people leave the row from the right end, what is B's new rank from the right?**
practice.solution: The 4 departed were to B's right (positions 1-4 from the right); B slides right-ward in rank: $12 - 4$ = **8th** from the right.
practice.shortcut: Exits on the side you are counting from subtract; the other side changes nothing.
